summary: Register or clear the repo's worktree setup command
examples: corral repo set-setup-command --repo corral --command 'npm ci --prefix app && npm ci --prefix mobile'
notes: Local host only. Remote routing: LIFE-403. Agent launch: LIFE-394. Archive hooks are not supported.
--command is one non-blank line without NUL or line breaks, at most 4096 bytes; null removes the command. An invalid value is refused before anything is written.

Setup command (LIFE-813): a repo's setup command is the one line registered with corral repo set-setup-command and stored in that repo's record in repos.json — nothing inside the repository (orca.yaml, conductor.json, .corral/) is ever read or run, and a newly added repo has none (setupCommand null). A value edited by hand in repos.json is checked by the same rule before it runs; an invalid one is refused with setup_command_invalid and never run. It runs as /bin/sh -c <command> in its own process group with cwd = the worktree, stdin closed, CORRAL_WORKTREE_PATH = the worktree and CORRAL_ROOT_PATH = the repo's main checkout, and PATH taken from the user's login shell ($SHELL -ilc, given at most a third of the budget and 5 s; receipt pathSource login_shell, or process when that probe fails or runs out). stdout and stderr go to one log file under <userData>/logs/worktree-setup/, never into the worktree; the receipt carries policy, status (completed, failed, timed_out or skipped), error (setup_failed, setup_timed_out or null), detail, exitCode, signal, durationMs and logPath. It runs inside the request budget (--timeout-ms, default 10000, at most 120000; about one second is kept back to report): past it the whole process group is killed and the result is timed_out. The default is too short for installs — give npm ci and the like --timeout-ms 120000. A cancelled request or a closing runtime kills the group at once. Processes that leave the group (setsid) and background children still running after the command exits normally are not killed. While the command runs, other workspace mutations (create, set, rm, repo changes) wait behind it; workspace reads (repo list/show, worktree list/show/current/ps) do not. A setup command that itself calls a corral workspace mutation on the same profile therefore waits until the budget runs out.

summary: Create a new corral-managed worktree
examples: corral worktree create --name LIFE-394-spike --repo corral --agent codex --effort high --prompt "start from specs/00-project.md" --timeout-ms 600000 --json
corral worktree create --name LIFE-603-start --repo corral --agent claude --prompt-file prompt.md --draft --request-id <id> --timeout-ms 120000 --json
notes: Local host only. Remote routing: LIFE-403. Archive hooks are not supported.

--setup inherit (default) runs the registered setup command when the repo has one and does nothing otherwise; --setup skip never runs it; --setup run requires one and is refused with setup_not_configured before git runs when there is none. The command runs after git worktree add and before --activate and any terminal stage, and the request waits for it. A failed or timed-out setup never removes the worktree or branch and is not retried: without --agent the request fails with setup_failed or setup_timed_out and resources path, branch, logPath and setupReceipt; with --agent the request still succeeds (exit 0, outcome completed) and stages.setup is the authoritative answer — failed with error setup_failed or setup_timed_out, reason and logPath — while the terminal, agent and prompt stages still run. With --request-id (with or without --agent) the result, including a setup failure, is recorded: the same id returns it again and never runs the command a second time, even after the worktree was removed. --run-hooks is not supported.

--agent claude|codex|grok synthesizes terminal create --agent in the new worktree after git succeeds; it is the same command and the same contract, not a second launch path. --model/--effort/--advisor/--prompt/--prompt-file require --agent and --advisor applies to --agent claude only. --prompt-file is resolved against the directory this command was invoked in, not the new worktree, and is read before the receipt is admitted and before git runs: an unreadable file is an effect-free invalid_argument, the body is part of the receipt fingerprint so the same request id with a changed file is request_conflict rather than a replay, and the child receives the verified body rather than the path.

Stages are reported one by one (worktree, terminal, agent, prompt) with status completed, queued, unknown, failed or not_started, and each stage keeps the handle and child request id it reached. A created git worktree is never removed because a later stage failed, and a stage whose effect is unobserved stays unknown and is not retried. stages.*.status is the authoritative answer: the synthesized top-level outcome is the coarser of the two and reads unknown when ANY stage is unknown, so an effect-free agent rejection (a refused submission, an unverified detect manifest) can sit under an outcome of unknown that belongs to a different stage. Read the stage before deciding what to retry.

Replay is by request id: the same --request-id replays the same partial result instead of re-running finished stages, failing with already_exists or creating a second terminal. Child stages derive their ids from it, so the composition is deterministic across runtime restarts.

--draft (LIFE-603) requires --agent and --prompt or --prompt-file. After the same ready gate as a submitted prompt, the body is written into the agent's input once as a bracketed paste and Enter is never sent. The body is sanitized first: CR and CRLF become LF, every other control character except LF and tab is dropped (including ESC, so a paste-end sequence in the body cannot close the paste early), and trailing whitespace is trimmed. stages.prompt then reports mode draft: completed with enterSent false means corral wrote the paste once while the agent's state was unchanged since the ready observation; it does not mean the text is visible in the input or that the provider did not submit it — only the provider's session record answers that, and this command does not read it. A blocking screen, an unverified detect manifest or a not-ready agent leaves stages.prompt not_started with the reason and writes nothing. Replaying the same --request-id returns the recorded result and does not type the draft again. Without --draft, --prompt keeps submitting once at ready.
